text: When Johnson came to set Shakespeare above the dramatists of his own age, he rested the preference on a single ground, and he stated it with his usual firmness: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature." (Johnson 1765) The persons of lesser playwrights, as he saw them, were cut to the fashions of a particular town and a particular season. They spoke the idiom of a coterie and acted on motives that depended on customs long since abandoned, and when the customs passed away the persons passed with them. Shakespeare's characters are of another kind. They are moved by passions which every reader has felt in himself or watched in others; their manners belong to no one court, street, or generation; and what is local in them is the dress and the phrasing, while the heart beneath is common to all. A reader who knows nothing of the theatre for which the plays were written can therefore open them and recognise at once what he finds there. A father's rage at an ungrateful daughter, a son's grief for a dead father, a husband's jealousy worked up out of a handkerchief: these still read as true.
